# A Supervisory Control Strategy of Distributed Drive Electric Vehicles for Coordinating Handling, Lateral Stability, and Energy Efficiency

Ningyuan Guo, Xudong Zhang, Yuan Zou, Basilio Lenzo, Guodong Du, and Tao Zhang

**Abstract: A supervisory control strategy, including dynamic control supervisor, handling-stability controller, energy efficiency controller, and coordinated torque allocator, is proposed for distributed drive electric vehicles to coordinate vehicle handling, lateral stability, and energy economy performance. In the dynamic control supervisor, firstly phase plane analysis is implemented to accurately define the vehicle stability boundary so that the look-up table of bounds can be established for online application. Subsequently, based on the feedback drive conditions and vehicle states, the identified boundary is dynamically quantified by the designed varying weight factor (VWF) in real time. In the handling-stability controller, a unified yaw rate reference of VWF is developed to simultaneously guarantee vehicle manoeuvrability and lateral stabilization. Then, a novel integral triple-steps method is proposed to calculate the proper direct yaw moment for the desired vehicle motion. In the energy efficiency controller, inter-axle torque distribution map is optimized for optimal vehicle energy economy. In the coordinated torque allocator, a torque increment allocation problem is formulated and optimized to realize the desired forces, meanwhile based on VWF to minimize energy consumption and tire workload usage. The validations of proposed strategy are conducted under various manoeuvres, yielding comprehensive improvements in terms of vehicle handling, lateral stability, and energy performance.**

**Keywords: distributed drive electric vehicles; supervision mechanism; unified yaw rate reference; energy efficiency; coordinated control.**

## I. INTRODUCTION

Distributed drive electric vehicles (DDEV) equipped with four in-wheel motors (IWM) have attracted enormous attention in the literature and industry. Compared with traditional centre-traction vehicles, a DDEV is an overactuated system that allows the independent control of each actuator. Such feature can be exploited to design advanced controllers to significantly enhance vehicle dynamics and energy efficiency [1]. On the other hand, the combination of such over-actuation with highly nonlinear vehicle dynamics is very challenging from the controller design perspective [2].

Many studies have been carried out in the past decades. In [3], a direct yaw moment control (DYC) is achieved by the second-order sliding mode control (SMC) method, and a rulebased control allocation is designed for torque distribution. In [4], a gain scheduled robust linear quadratic regulator (LQR) is proposed for DYC to limit the closed-loop tracking error and overcome system uncertainties and disturbances. In [5, 6], a linear matrix inequality based Hinf controller is designed to synthetically govern active front steering and DYC for vehicle stability. In [7], an adaptive SMC with linear matrix inequality-based switching surfaces is designed for vehicle stability, where the uncertain term and switching control gain are dynamically regulated by fuzzy logic. Considering fault tolerations, linear parameter-varying Hinf techniques are adopted in [8, 9] for robust active front steering (AFS) of DDEVs. In [10], a model predictive control-based scheme is developed to enhance vehicle stability and energy economy;

however, energy efficiency improvements are achieved by decreasing the generated yaw moment, which potentially induces risks of vehicle instability. In [11], a dynamic SMC is delegated to compute the external yaw moment, and an adaptive energy-efficient control allocation is proposed by Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions for optimal torque distribution. To coordinate energy efficiency and vehicle motion, a holistic cornering control (HCC) is proposed in [12]. It is a concise and modular approach to implement the superior dynamic trade-offs between vehicle motion and energy efficiency.

The above studies mainly focus on vehicle stability control and/or energy economy. It is noteworthy that vehicle handling is also critically important for desirable vehicle performance and driver experience, and that bad handling may potentially cause the loss of vehicle stability [13]. For instance, under extreme driving conditions, the tires may skid, and novice drivers may perform incorrect operations due to panic, possibly resulting in accidents [14]. DYC is a largely used approach to control planar motion of DDEVs [15]. Desired handling and stability criteria are typically achieved through single-input-multiple-output (SIMO) DYC control formulations, but often outputs are hard to be stabilized simultaneously. In [16], a single-input-singleoutput (SISO) reference yaw rate is proposed that yields effective in conducting two objectives during DYC, i.e., controlling yaw rate and sideslip angle. In [17], the expected driver intentions are quantitatively described by simulation data, and a control-mode-switching approach is devoted to harmonize vehicle handling and stability.

In light of the above contributions, DDEV control strategies seldom consider the coordination of handling, lateral stability, and energy efficiency requirements. To this end, the idea of supervisory control strategy has gradually risen, which commonly involves a supervision mechanism to trade off each target in a synergetic manner [18]. In earlier studies [19, 20], the so-called supervisor mainly decides the activation of vehicle stability control to avoid unnecessary interferences with the driver. In [20], the tracking errors of yaw rate and sideslip angle are respectively used in the calculation of two indices to manage the status “ON/OFF” of DYC, where the controller activates when one index is greater than a threshold. Another similar example can be found in [21], with an approach that again avoids unnecessary interferences with the driver, but only targeting vehicle stability. Besides, the simple Boolean activation of DYC leads to motor torque command chattering [21], thereby hindering drive comfort and motor lifetime. In [22], a superior supervisor is developed which divides the current vehicle status into three types, so that independent AFS and DYC controllers can contribute to stabilize the vehicle in a coordinated manner. In [23], the sideslip angle-sideslip angle rate phase plane portrait analysis contributes to design a weight factor for coordinating the coupled effects of differential drive assist steering and vehicle motion. Only the vehicle velocity and tire-road friction are adopted to define the stability regions, while the influence of the front wheel steering angle is neglected thus limiting the accuracy of stability assessment [24]. Similarly, based on phase plane portrait analysis, Ref. [25] proposes a supervisory strategy for stability, handling, and energy efficiency, including a LQR controller and a rule-based torque allocation. Although a superior performance is yielded, the energy efficiency aspect is dealt with through an experience-based method, and the effects of tire nonlinearities and tire-road friction limits are not considered, leaving room for the development of highperformance supervisory control.

Indeed, phase plane portrait analysis is an effective tool to determine the stable region, so that the supervisory control strategy can be developed for coordination control of different objectives. Its main idea is to accurately determine the stable bounds offline, that is adopted in online supervising vehicle states for trading off each target via the controller. A widely used approach is the two-lines method [23-25], which defines the stable region by two lines crossing the saddle points in the sideslip angle-sideslip angle rate phase plane portrait. However, it still includes the unstable region that corresponds to the vehicle lateral acceleration out of the limits and is unable to accurately decide the stable bounds. Moreover, part of the stable region defined by the two-lines method lies on the tire nonlinear range; that is, for this region the targets of handling and stability are still not consistent, entailing undesired effects in the supervisory strategy (see more details in Section 3.2.1). Given these, the stable region is defined as ellipses in Ref. [22], but it requires enormous burden in terms of calibration of polynomial fitting, that limits its application.

To fill above gaps, this paper proposes a supervisory control strategy for coordinating handling, lateral stability, and energy efficiency. There proposed strategy consists of four parts: 1) a dynamic control supervisor; 2) an handlingstability controller; 3) an energy efficiency controller; and 4) a coordinated torque allocator. It is noteworthy that the proposed strategy is not a simple combination of controllers of different target, but achieves each target in a systematic manner. Each module in the proposed strategy is coupled to others, so that superior coordinated control effects can be achieved. Moreover, from a practical point of view, the design processes of each module are concise and straightforward, thus this developed scheme is easy to understand and implement by engineers. The main contributions of this paper are:

1) In the dynamic control supervisor, the sideslip anglesideslip angle rate phase plane analysis is used to graphically develop the stable region of vehicle motion. Beyond commonly included factors (i.e., the vehicle velocity and the tire-road friction), the front-wheel steering angle, the maximum allowable lateral acceleration, and phase plane region that conflicts between handling and stability objectives, are considered. In addition, the fitting approximations are not required in stable bounds’ calibrations by the proposed method, which considerably reduces the design workloads. After calibration, a look-up table based on the stable boundaries is built for online application. During driving, according to the current driving conditions and vehicle state, the stable boundaries can be dynamically quantified as a varying weight factor (VWF) to govern the supervisory control strategy.

2) In the handling-stability controller, a unified yaw rate reference determined by VWF is developed to simultaneously achieve vehicle stability and handling in a smooth manner. The integral triple-steps method (ITSM) is proposed as DYC method for tracking the target yaw motion. Unlike traditional triple-steps method, the integral gain item is incorporated so that the static tracking errors can be reduced.

3) In the energy efficiency controller, the energy efficient inter-axle problem is formulated and optimized to be a map under the assumption of small battery power losses. Its effectiveness to find the globally optimal solution is strictly proved by Pontryagin’s minimum principle (PMP).

4) In the coordinated torque allocator, the torque increments are optimized so as to achieve the expected forces at each IWM and, at the same time, to minimize the energy consumption and tire workload usage by VWF.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the adopted vehicle and tire model, along with the electric power flows of the powertrain. The supervisory control strategy is described in Section III, and simulation results are discussed in Section IV. The key conclusions of this paper are summarized in Section V.

## II. MODELLING OF THE DDEV

## 2.1. Vehicle Dynamics Model

The studied vehicle is a front-wheel steering DDEV, depicted in Fig. 1. To characterize its dynamics, the singletrack vehicle model is adopted:

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} m _ {v} \left(\dot {v} _ {y} + v _ {x} \gamma\right) = F _ {y f} + F _ {y r} \\ I _ {z} \dot {\gamma} = l _ {a} F _ {y f} - l _ {b} F _ {y r} + \Delta M _ {z} \end{array} \right.\tag{1}
$$

where $m _ { _ { y } } , l _ { _ { a } } , l _ { _ { b } }$ , and $I _ { z }$ are respectively the total vehicle mass, the distance from front axle to the center of gravity (CG), the distance from rear axle to CG, and the vehicle yaw moment of inertia. $\nu _ { x }$ and $\nu _ { y }$ represent the longitudinal and lateral velocity of the vehicle CG. is the vehicle yaw rate, $\Delta M _ { z }$ is the external yaw moment applied by the controller, and in the system of Eq. (1) the external disturbance is the driver steering angle , influencing the tire lateral forces.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 1. DDEV schematic.

Under the assumption of small values of vehicle sideslip angle $\beta$ , we have

$$
\beta = \arctan (v _ {y} / v _ {x}) \approx v _ {y} / v _ {x}\tag{2}
$$

$F _ { y f }$ and $F _ { y r }$ represent the lateral forces of front and rear axles, respectively. They are expressed as

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} F _ {y f} = F _ {y 1} + F _ {y 2} \\ F _ {y r} = F _ {y 3} + F _ {y 4} \end{array} \right.\tag{3}
$$

where the subscripts of “1”, “2”, “3”, and $^ { \circ } 4 ^ { \circ }$ express that the corresponding variables are related to front-left, front-right, rear-left and rear-right wheels, respectively and hereinafter. The lateral force $F _ { y i }$ at each wheel is calculated through the Magic Formula [26]:

$$
\begin{array}{l} F _ {y i} = \phi_ {M F} (\alpha , \mu , F _ {z i}) \\ \quad = D _ {o} \sin \left[ C _ {o} \arctan \left\{B _ {o} \alpha - E _ {o} \left(B _ {o} \alpha - \arctan (B _ {o} \alpha)\right) \right\} \right] \end{array}\tag{4}
$$

where $D _ { _ o } = \mu F _ { _ z }$ is the peak side force, $\mu$ is the tire-road friction factor, and $F _ { z i }$ is the vertical load at the i-th wheel. $C_{F \alpha} = B_{o}C_{o}D_{o} = c_{F \alpha}F_{z i}$ is the tire cornering stiffness. $\mathcal { C } _ { F \alpha }$ is a shape coefficient. In Eq. (4), the slip angles of front and rear

tires, i.e., $\alpha _ { f }$ and $\alpha _ { r }$ , are:

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} \alpha_ {f} = \delta - (v _ {y} + l _ {a} \gamma) / v _ {x} = \delta - (\beta + l _ {a} \gamma / v _ {x}) \\ \alpha_ {r} = (l _ {b} \gamma - v _ {y}) / v _ {x} = l _ {b} \gamma / v _ {x} - \beta \end{array} \right.\tag{5}
$$

where $\delta$ is the steering angle of front wheels. From Eqs. (1) to (5), we can express the control-oriented vehicle dynamics model as

$$
\left[ \begin{array}{c} \dot {\beta} \\ \dot {\gamma} \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{c} \frac {2 \left(\phi_ {M F} \left(\alpha_ {f} , \mu , F _ {z f}\right) + \phi_ {M F} \left(\alpha_ {r} , \mu , F _ {z r}\right)\right)}{m _ {v} v _ {x}} - \gamma \\ \frac {2 \left(l _ {a} \phi_ {M F} \left(\alpha_ {f} , \mu , F _ {z f}\right) - l _ {b} \phi_ {M F} \left(\alpha_ {r} , \mu , F _ {z r}\right)\right)}{I _ {z}} + \frac {\Delta M _ {z}}{I _ {z}} \end{array} \right]\tag{6}
$$

where the vector including $\beta$ and is the state variable, $\Delta M _ { z }$ is the control variable, and the front wheel steering angle $\delta$ is considered as the external disturbance. To obtain sideslip angle, tire-road friction factor, and longitudinal velocity, extensive studies of advanced estimators [27, 28] have been carried out for satisfactory accuracy, thus these variables are assumed to be real-time obtainable. Moreover, the yaw rate can easily be measured by inertial measurement unit (IMU) in practice and thus is also assumed to be obtainable here.

## 2.2. Electric Power Flow Model

The first-order internal resistance equivalent-circuit model [29, 30] is adopted to reflect the battery charge dynamics:

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} U _ {t} = U _ {o} - I _ {b} R _ {o} \\ S O C = S O C _ {o} - \int \frac {I _ {b}}{3 6 0 0 Q _ {b}} d t \end{array} \right.\tag{7}
$$

where $U _ { t }$ and $I _ { b }$ are the battery terminal voltage and current, respectively. $U _ { o }$ and $R _ { o }$ represent the open-circuit voltage and the internal resistance, respectively, which are determined by look-up tables of the battery state-of-charge (SOC) [31]. SOC and $S O C _ { o }$ are the current SOC and the initial SOC, respectively. $\mathcal { Q } _ { b }$ is the battery charge capacity. From Eq. (7), the battery power can be written as

$$
P _ {b o} = P _ {b i} - P _ {l o s s} = U _ {t} I _ {b} = U _ {o} I _ {b} - I _ {b} ^ {2} R _ {o}\tag{8}
$$

where $P _ { b o }$ and $P _ { b i }$ are the battery output and input power, respectively. The four IWMs in this paper are identical, and the power of one motor $P _ { m }$ can expressed:

$$
P _ {m} = T _ {m} \omega_ {m}\tag{9}
$$

where $T _ { m }$ and $\omega _ { m }$ are the motor torque and speed, respectively. The electric-coupled relationship between battery and motors is:

$$
P _ {b o} = P _ {m} / \eta_ {m} (T _ {m}, \omega_ {m}) ^ {\text {sign} (T _ {m})}\tag{10}
$$

where $\eta _ { m } ( \cdot , \cdot )$ is the motor efficiency, depending on torque and speed, as shown in Fig. 3. To satisfy the physical capacity of motor, the torque limits of speed are imposed, as shown in Fig. 3, i.e.

$$
\underline {{T _ {m}}} (\omega_ {m}) \leq T _ {m} \leq \overline {{T _ {m}}} (\omega_ {m})\tag{11}
$$

where $\overline { { 0 } }$ and $\underbrace { 0 }$ mean the maximum and minimum limits of the specified variable, respectively.

**Remark 1**: There inevitably exist time delays due to the motor dynamic responses. In this paper, this response feature is simulated as a first-order inertia element module of time constant 0.01 s in a Matlab/Simulink validation model, but

## III. SUPERVISORY CONTROL STRATEGY

## 3.1. Control Framework

The control framework of the supervisory strategy, illustrated in Fig. 2, includes four main elements:

1) Dynamic Control Supervisor: The phase plane analysis is conducted to work out the look-up table that can dynamically identify the vehicle stability boundary in real time. Beyond traditionally considered factors (i.e., vehicle velocity and tire-road friction), here the front-wheel steering angle, the maximum allowable acceleration, and phase plane region that conflicts between handling and stability objectives, are considered for enhanced supervisor effects. An appropriate index regarding the identified boundary and the vehicle states is developed and transformed as VWF to govern the supervisory strategy.

2) Handling-Stability Controller: By the VWF, a unified yaw rate reference is designed that can smoothly achieve vehicle manoeuvrability and lateral stabilization. A nonlinear DYC controller is employed to track the target yaw motion while coping with tire nonlinearities and restricting static errors.

3) Energy Efficiency Controller: According to the vehicle velocity and total traction torque (from driver), the energy efficient inter-axle torque allocation problem is constructed and optimized under the assumption of small battery power losses. Then, a map of optimal distribution ratio can be obtained for online application.

4) Coordinated Torque Allocator: The objectives of the virtual controls (i.e., longitudinal and DYC torque targets), the energy efficiency, and the tire workload usage, are all considered for an individual torque increment allocation with the constraints of tire-road adhesion limits and motor actuation capacity. For this multi-objective optimization problem, the VWF coordinates the targets of energy efficiency and tire workload usage. Finally, by summing up the inter-axle torques and the optimized torque increments, the torque commands of IWMs are sent to the high-fidelity vehicle model in CarSim®.

## 3.2. Dynamic Control Supervisor

## 3.2.1. Phase Plane Portrait Analysis

The phase plane portrait can vividly reflect the system stability status. After plotting the phase trajectories and equilibrium points, the vehicle system dynamics and steadystate effects can be observed, hence it is an appropriate approach to study the stable region for vehicle motion supervisor design [32]. Fig. 4 depicts the $\beta   -   \dot { \beta }$ phase plane result with velocity of 20 m/s, tire-road friction factor of 1, and front wheel steering angle of 0 rad, 0.0698 rad, and 0.1396 rad. As shown in Fig. 4 (a), when the steering angle is 0 rad, the phase trajectories are symmetric with respect to the origin. The saddle points are symmetrically located with respect to the origin on the $\dot { \beta }$ axis, and the stable region, where trajectories converge to stable point, mainly lies on the second and fourth quadrants. From Fig. 4 (a) and Fig. 4 (b), as the steering angle increases, the stable and saddle points move towards greater values of sideslip angle. When the steering angle reaches 0.1396 rad, as shown in Fig. 4 (c), the stable point and the left saddle point disappear, and no stable region exists, meaning that the vehicle has already lost its stability.

To definitely classify the convergent regions, some papers apply the two-lines methods [20, 23], as shown by the red lines in Fig. 4. The two red lines intersect the saddle points, one for a positive sideslip angle, one for a negative sideslip angle, and the stable region is defined as the area between the two lines. The requirements to determine one red line in the positive/negative side of the $\beta$ axis are crossing the saddle point and adjoining the bound that can distinguish the phase trajectories of converging and diverging to the stable point. The two-lines method is simple and relatively easy to operate but shows two drawbacks in accurately defining the stable region and coordination control:

1) Vehicle Stability: When the yaw rate tends to its maximum or minimum, the lateral tire forces are possibly close to saturation, and tire skid may happen thus causing potential vehicle instability. In particular, a novice driver may perform incorrect operations to further hinder vehicle stabilization due to panic [33]. This case can also be reflected in the phase plane portrait of vehicle. Here the widely-used limits of yaw rate in vehicle stabilization can be adopted, i.e., $\gamma \leq \left| \mu g / v_{_x} \right|$ . By inputting the limit values into the first

expression of Eq. (6), the $\beta   -   \dot { \beta }$ phase trajectories regarding maximum/minimum yaw rate can be plotted, as shown in the blue and green lines of Fig. 4. One can find that there is still an unstable area outside the maximum/minimum yaw rate and inside the boundaries by two-lines method. Hence it is preferable to remove this unstable area from that by two-lines method.

2) Conflicts between Stability and Handling: Based on the handling reference of yaw rate (i.e., Eq. (16) that is the equilibrium point via solving linear single-track vehicle model [34]) in Fig. 4 (a), the increase of sideslip angle is limited along the handling reference when the absolute sideslip angle is small (i.e., $| \beta | \leq 0 . 1 5 \mathrm { r a d } )$ . From [33, 35], in the $\beta   -   \dot { \beta }$ phase plane, the lower is the slope of the trajectory $d \dot { \beta } / d \beta$ , the stronger the restriction effects are. Combining with Fig. 4 (a), when $\left| \beta \right|   \le   0 . 1 5$ rad and along with the handling reference, the slope of trajectory is much less than $0 ,$ which means that rather strong restriction effects are imposed to avoid the enlargement of sideslip angle. Instead, when $| \beta | > 0.15   rad$ , the slope becomes gentle and slightly greater than 0. That is, if $\left| \beta \right|   \leq   0 . 1 5$ rad, tracking handling reference can also effectively stabilize the vehicle, and the control conflicts between stability and handling can be avoided.

Based on above analysis, a modified approach is proposed to more precisely assess the vehicle stability, representing the stable bounds with purple lines in Fig. 4. The narrower bounds of sideslip angle aim to define a more accurate region to avoid conflicts in control of handling and stability. The yaw rate is bounded at $\gamma   =   \pm \mu g   /   \nu _ { j }$ (derived from the allowable maximal lateral acceleration [36]), thus avoiding potential skidding. The proposed stable region can be summed up as:

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} \beta_ {\min} \leq \beta \leq \beta_ {\max} \\ \gamma_ {\min} \leq \gamma \leq \gamma_ {\max} \end{array} \right.\tag{12}
$$

In Eq. (12), $\gamma _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ and $\gamma _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ are directly calculated by $\pm \mu g / v_{x} . \beta_{\min}$ and $\beta _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ are actually the -axis positions of saddle points, which can be obtained by solving the differential equation Eq. (6) with different vehicle velocity, tire-road friction factor, and front wheel steering angle. When the stable region disappears, like Fig. $4 \mathrm { ~ \bf ~ ( c ) } ,$ we set $\beta_{\min} = \beta_{\max} = 0$ For ease of strategy application, the calculated values of $\beta _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ and $\beta _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ are stored as a 3-D lookup table in this paper. By this manner, the two drawbacks of the two-lines method mentioned above can be overcome, and meanwhile the burden in offline calibrations of the stable bounds can be considerably reduced since only the axis positions of the saddle points are needed, which can be obtained by solving the differential equations of $\beta$ , Eq. (6), imposing that the time derivatives of sideslip angle and yaw rate are zero. Fig. 5 shows the results of $\beta _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ and $\beta _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ . The stable region shrinks with decreasing tire-road friction factor and increasing vehicle velocity, which is consistent with the fact that more likely risks of vehicle accidents exist under lower road friction and higher velocity.

## 3.2.2. Varying Weight Factor Design

Although a precise stable region is defined, it cannot be directly delegated into the supervisory control strategy. To do so, two evaluation indexes are set to quantitatively describe the vehicle status according to Eq. (12):

$$
I _ {\beta} = 1 - \operatorname{sign} \left(\left(\beta_ {\max} - \beta\right) \left(\beta - \beta_ {\min}\right)\right) \frac {\min \left(\left| \beta_ {\max} - \beta \right| , \left| \beta - \beta_ {\min} \right|\right)}{\left(\beta_ {\max} - \beta_ {\min}\right) / 2}\tag{13}
$$

$$
I _ {\gamma} = 1 - \mathrm{sign} \big ((\gamma_ {\max} - \gamma) (\gamma - \gamma_ {\min}) \big) \frac {\min (| \gamma_ {\max} - \gamma | , | \gamma - \gamma_ {\min} |)}{(\gamma_ {\max} - \gamma_ {\min}) / 2}\tag{14}
$$

where $I _ { \beta }$ and $I _ { \gamma }$ are the evaluation indexes regarding $\beta$ and $\gamma$ , respectively. By Eqs. (13) and (14), the shortest distance between the current vehicle states and the boundaries can be assessed. Fig. 6 (a) shows an example of the expression in the form of Eqs. (13) and (14), where an independent variable with allowed range of -2 to 4 is studied. The index minimum is 0 (signifying that $q$ is at the maximum distance from both bounds), and it is not allowed to exceed 1 since value 1 in indexes $I _ { \beta }$ and $I _ { \gamma }$ corresponds to the allowed bound.

To unify $I _ { \beta }$ and $I _ { \gamma }$ , the vehicle stability evaluation index $I _ { u n i f i e d }$ is defined as $I_{unified} = \max(I_{\beta}, I_{\gamma})$ , and a smoothed VWF can be developed [37]:

$$
\rho \left(I _ {\text {unified}}\right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 0 & , 0 \leq I _ {\text {unified}} <   0. 7 \\ \frac {1}{2} \left(1 - \cos \left(\pi \frac {I _ {\text {unified}} - 0 . 7}{1 - 0 . 7}\right)\right) & , 0. 7 \leq I _ {\text {unified}} \leq 1 \end{array} \right.\tag{15}
$$

## 3.3. Handling-Stability Controller

## 3.3.1. Unified Yaw Rate Reference

As mentioned in Section I, the addressed system of vehicle motion control is SIMO and cannot be stabilized by only one reference. To do this, a unified yaw rate reference is proposed in this section. To guarantee the vehicle handling, the yaw rate reference $\gamma _ { h }$ can be expressed as [38]:

$$
\gamma_ {h} = v _ {x} \delta / \left(l _ {a} + l _ {b}\right) + \kappa v _ {x} ^ {2})\tag{16}
$$

where is the understeer gradient and equals to $m_{v}(l_{b}C_{r}-l_{a}C_{f})/(2C_{f}C_{r}(l_{a}+l_{b})^{2})$ . Only the linear tire cornering stiffness of the front and rear wheels (namely $C _ { f }$ and $C _ { r } )$ is employed in to guarantee a consistent handling experience for drivers.

Based on vehicle kinematics $\gamma = \frac { a _ { y } } { v _ { x } } + \dot { \beta } \approx \frac { a _ { y } } { v _ { x } }$ [16], the stable reference is defined by the yaw rate [39]:

$$
\gamma_ {s} = a _ {y} / v _ {x}\tag{17}
$$

where $a _ { y } = \dot { \nu } _ { y } + \nu _ { x } \gamma$ is the lateral vehicle acceleration and can be measured by an IMU. From $\gamma _ { h }$ and $\gamma _ { s }$ , the unified yaw rate reference $\gamma _ { r e f }$ is set up by the VWF $\rho$ in the form of weight sum:

$$
\gamma_ {r e f} = \rho \gamma_ {s} + (1 - \rho) \gamma_ {h}\tag{18}
$$

The unified yaw rate reference by Eq. (18) is dynamically varying according to the VWF $\rho$ regarding current vehicle states, as mentioned in Remark 6. Therefore, the conflicts between control of handling and stability can be effectively resolved by the proposed reference of Eq. (18).

## 3.3.2. Nonlinear Controller Design by Integral Triple-steps Method

The nonlinear controller ITSM consisting of steady-state control, feedforward control, and feedback control, is developed for DYC. It is easily understandable and can be seen as a specific proportional-integral (PI) controller, thus suitable for generalization in engineering application. Moreover, thanks to the steady-state, feedforward, and feedback items in control law, the high system performance can be guaranteed [40]. Before addressing the controller design, the control-oriented model of DYC should be set up. Different from the traditional DYC that needs to simultaneously stabilize sideslip angle and yaw rate, the unified yaw reference in Eq. (18) can be adopted, by tracking which the coordination of handling and stability is achievable. In other words, the control-oriented model of vehicle motion can be established as a SISO system regarding only one state, i.e., , whose expression is yielded according to vehicle dynamics (6):

$$
\dot {\gamma} = g (x) + Q u\tag{19}
$$

where $g(x) = 2\left(l_{a}\phi_{MF}(\alpha_{f},\mu,F_{zf}) - l_{b}\phi_{MF}(\alpha_{r},\mu,F_{zr})\right)/I_{z}$ $Q = 1 / I_z , u = \Delta M_z$ is the control variable and same with that in Eq. (6). Given Eq. (19), the design procedure by ITSM is described as follows.

1) Steady-state Control: Assuming that the current yaw rate is steady-state and $u = u _ { _ s }$ , the steady-state control $u _ { s }$ can be obtained by setting $\dot { \gamma }   =   0$ of Eq. (19) and expressed as

$$
u _ {s} = - g (x) / Q\tag{20}
$$

2) Feedforward Control: To improve the transient effects and restriction capacity in external disturbances and/or inaccurate model parameters, one can set $u   =   u _ { _ s }   +   u _ { _ f }$ , where $u _ { f }$ is a feedforward control. Combining the new with Eq. (19), it is $\dot { \gamma }   =   Q u _ { f }$ . Set $\dot { \gamma }   =   \dot { \gamma } _ { r e f }$ , then

$$
u _ {f} = \dot {\gamma} _ {r e f} / Q\tag{21}
$$

3) Feedback Control: To enhance the robustness and errorrestriction capacity, the feedback control is indispensable. Set $u = u _ { s } + u _ { f } + u _ { e }$ and insert into Eq. (19) again:

$$
\dot {\gamma} = \dot {\gamma} _ {r e f} + Q u _ {e}\tag{22}
$$

The error system can be defined as $e   =   \gamma _ { \mathit { r e f } } - \gamma$ , and based on Eq. (22), its differential is $\dot { e }   =   \dot { \gamma } _ { r e f }   -   \dot { \gamma }   =   - Q u _ { e }$ . Defining the Lyapunov function as $V = \frac{1}{2}e^{2} + \frac{1}{2}k_{0}\chi^{2}, \quad \chi = \int edt$ , and the coefficient $k _ { 0 }   \mathrm { > } 0$ , it is

$$
\dot {V} = e \dot {e} + k _ {0} \chi e = - Q u _ {e} e + k _ {0} \chi e\tag{23}
$$

Obviously, setting $u _ { e } = ( k _ { 1 } e + k _ { 0 } \chi ) / Q$ and the coefficient $k _ { 1 }   \mathrm { ~ \textgreater 0 ~ }$ can make the system asymptotically stable, namely $\dot { V } = e \dot { e } + k _ { 0 } \chi e = - k _ { 1 } e ^ { 2 } \leq 0$ . From above steps 1) to 3), the control law of ITSM can be sorted as

$$
\begin{array}{l} u = \Delta M _ {z} = u _ {s} + u _ {f} + u _ {e} = - 2 \left(l _ {a} \phi_ {M F} (\alpha_ {f}, \mu , F _ {z f}) - l _ {b} \phi_ {M F} (\alpha_ {r}, \mu , F _ {z r})\right) \\ \quad + I _ {z} \dot {\gamma} _ {r e f} + k _ {1} I _ {z} (\gamma_ {r e f} - \gamma) + k _ {0} I _ {z} \int (\gamma_ {r e f} - \gamma) d t \end{array}\tag{24}
$$

**Remark 2:** The feedback control $u _ { e }$ in Eq. (24) is a PI controller, where $k _ { 1 } I _ { z }$ and $k _ { 0 } I _ { z }$ are the P-gain and I-gain coefficients, respectively. Compared with the triple-steps method in [40], the I-gain item is added into the control law to further reduce the static errors [41]. Moreover, when the current vehicle state is unstable, $\mathcal { Y } _ { r e f } = \mathcal { Y } _ { s }$ from Eq. (18). Based on the vehicle kinematics $\gamma = a _ { y } / \nu _ { x } + \dot { \beta }$ and Eq. (17), we have $- \dot { \beta } = a _ { y } / \nu _ { x } - \gamma = \gamma _ { s } - \gamma$ . By Eq. (24), the feedback control $u _ { e }$ in Eq. (24) can be calculated as $k_{1}I_{z}(0 - \dot{\beta}) + k_{0}I_{z}(0 - \beta)$ . This is a proportional-differential (PD) controller to make $\beta$ converging to 0, which means that $\beta$ is tracking a sideslip angle reference $\beta _ { r e f }$ of $0$ to restrict the $\beta$ enlargement.

## 3.4. Energy Efficiency Controller

Under longitudinal drive cycles, the four-wheel torque allocation problem is inter-axle since there is no DYC; that is, the torques at the right side and left side of an axle are the same. The torque relationships between each IWM and the total traction torque $T _ { t o t }$ is:

$$
\frac {T _ {f}}{2} = \frac {p T _ {t o t}}{2} = T _ {1} = T _ {2}, \frac {T _ {r}}{2} = \frac {(1 - p) T _ {t o t}}{2} = T _ {3} = T _ {4}\tag{25}
$$

where $T _ { 1 }   ,   T _ { 2 }   ,   T _ { 3 }$ , and $T _ { 4 }$ are the output torques regarding front-left, front-right, rear-left and rear-right IWMs, respectively. $p$ is the inter-axle allocation ratio within 0 to 1. Neglecting the tire slips, the rotational speed of wheels is expressed as $\omega_{1}=\omega_{2}=\omega_{3}=\omega_{4}=\omega_{m}=\frac{V_{x}}{r_{w}}$ , where $r _ { w }$ represents the wheel radius. Additionally, the power loss of the battery from warming of internal resistance is extremely small and can be ignored for simplification [42], namely $P _ { \mathit { l o s s } } \approx 0$ . From Eqs. (8) to (10), the total energy consumption $E _ { t o t }$ of the battery through one cycle is:

$$
\begin{array}{c} E _ {t o t} = \int P _ {b i} d t = \int P _ {b o} + P _ {l o s s} d t \approx \int P _ {b o} d t \\ = \int (\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {4} T _ {i} \omega_ {i} / \eta_ {m} (T _ {i}, \omega_ {i}) ^ {\mathrm{sign} (T _ {i})}) d t \end{array}\tag{26}
$$

The minimization of $E _ { t o t }$ is equivalent to minimize $P _ { b o }$ per sample time, as explained in proposition 1 below. Thus, the optimization problem of energy-efficient inter-axle control is expressed according to Eqs. (25) and (26), as

$$
p ^ {*} = \arg \min P _ {b o} \left(T _ {t o t}, v _ {x}\right) = \arg \min \left\{p T _ {t o t} v _ {x} / r _ {w} \eta_ {m} \left(\frac {p T _ {t o t}}{2}, \frac {v _ {x}}{r _ {w}}\right) ^ {\operatorname{sign} \left(\frac {p T _ {t o t}}{2}\right)} \right.
$$

$$
+ (1 - p) T _ {t o t} v _ {x} / r _ {w} \eta_ {m} \left(\frac {(1 - p) T _ {t o t}}{2}, \frac {v _ {x}}{r _ {w}}\right) ^ {\operatorname{sign} \left(\frac {(1 - p) T _ {t o t}}{2}\right)} \rbrace\tag{27}
$$

subject to Eqs. (11), (25), and

$$
0. 5 \leq p \leq 1\tag{28}
$$

Since front-wheel-drive vehicles exhibit an understeering behaviour, which is deemed safer than oversteering, larger torques of front axle are favoured, i.e., Eq. (28).

The optimization of Eq. (27) is only related to $T _ { t o t }$ and $\nu _ { x }$ By inputting different $T _ { t o t }$ and $\nu _ { x }$ , the optimal allocation ratio $p ^ { * }$ can be worked out and stored as a look-up table for practical applications, as illustrated in the calculation operations in Table I. The grids of $T _ { _ { t o t } } \mathrm { ~ , ~ } \nu _ { _ { x } }$ , and are [- 1200:10:1200] N m., [0:2.5:220] km/h, and $[ 0 . 5 { : } 0 . 0 1 { : } 1 ] ,$ respectively. Fig. 7 shows the map of optimized energyefficient inter-axle allocation ratio and its intuitive application schematic. At each sample instant, the vehicle speed and total traction torque $T _ { t o t }$ are obtained by system feedback and then input into the optimal inter-axle allocation ratio map to obtain the optimal allocation ratio $p ^ { * }$ . Based on $T _ { t o t }$ and $p ^ { * }$ , the torques of front and rear wheels for optimal energy efficiency can be calculated by Eq. (25).

Table I. Calculation Steps for Energy-Efficient Inter-axle Torque Allocation Ratio.

<div class="docvortex-algorithm" style="white-space: pre-wrap; font-family:monospace;">
Steps Operations
Given different $T_{tot}$, $v_x$, and $p$, with a constant grid interval, by Eqs. (8) to (10), and (25), the corresponding $P_{bo}$ can be acquired and stored as a three-dimensional matrix A.
From matrix A, for each couple of $T_{tot}$ and $v_x$, find the related $p^*$ minimizing $P_{bo}$ and satisfying $T_i \leq \overline{T_m}(v_x / r_w)$.
If $T_{tot} &lt; 4\underline{T_m}(v_x / r_w)$, set $p^* = 0.5$.
Repeat step 2) for all the possible combinations of $T_{tot}$ and $v_x$.
Finally, a two-dimensional matrix of $p^*$ related to $T_{tot}$ and $v_x$ can be obtained.
</div>

**Proposition 1:** According to PMP [43], that min $\int P_{bo}dt \Leftrightarrow \min P_{bo}$ is hold under the assumption of

$$
P _ {l o s s} \approx 0.
$$

**Proof:** Please see Appendix A for more details.

**Remark 3:** The total traction torque can be easily calculated via driver pedal opening positions [1]. For simplification, this signal is assumed to be pre-known and directly gained by the Carsim® driver model in this paper.

## 3.5. Coordinated Torque Allocator

To conduct the expected vehicle motions and energy efficiency, the coordinated allocator of torque increments is developed to distribute the virtual controls among IWMs. The final torque commands of IWMs are merged by torques from energy efficiency controller and coordinated torque allocator (see Fig. 2):

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} T _ {1} ^ {*} = T _ {1} + \Delta T _ {1}, T _ {2} ^ {*} = T _ {2} + \Delta T _ {2} \\ T _ {3} ^ {*} = T _ {3} + \Delta T _ {3}, T _ {4} ^ {*} = T _ {4} + \Delta T _ {4} \end{array} \right.\tag{29}
$$

where $T _ { i } ^ { * }$ is the final torque command of the i-th IWM, and $\Delta T _ { i }$ is the i-th IWM’s torque increment optimized by the coordinated torque allocator. For a simple description of the allocator, hereinafter we define the vector of final torque commands as $\boldsymbol { \varpi } ^ { * } = [ T _ { 1 } ^ { ^ { * } } \quad T _ { 2 } ^ { ^ { * } } \quad T _ { 3 } ^ { ^ { * } } \quad T _ { 4 } ^ { ^ { * } } ] ^ { T }$ , the vector of torques from energy efficiency controller as $\varpi = \left[ T_{1} \quad T_{2} \quad T_{3} \quad T_{4} \right]^T$ , and the vector of torque increments optimized by allocator as $\Delta \varpi = \left[ \Delta T_{1} \quad \Delta T_{2} \quad \Delta T_{3} \quad \Delta T_{4} \right]^T$ That is, Eq. (29) can also be expressed as $\varpi^{*} = \varpi + \Delta \varpi$ . In this paper, three targets, i.e., satisfying the virtual controls, minimizing the tire workload, and maximizing energy efficiency, are considered:

1) Virtual Controls: For expected vehicle drive effects, the virtual controls regarding longitudinal and yaw motions from driver and handling stability controller should be hold, namely

$$
\mathrm{K} \Delta \varpi = \upsilon\tag{30}
$$

where $\mathrm{K}=\left[\begin{aligned}&\left[1\quad1\quad1\quad1\right]\\d_{s}\left/\left(2r_{w}\right)\times\left[-1\quad1\quad-1\quad1\right]\right.\end{aligned}\right]$ is the stable gain, and $\boldsymbol { \upsilon }   =   [ 0 \quad \Delta M _ { z } ] ^ { T }$ is the virtual controls. $d _ { s }$ is the vehicle track width, and $r _ { w }$ is the effective radius of tires. In Eq. (30), the first and second elements on both sides of equal sign, are the required resultant torque increments and external yaw moment, respectively. Since $\sum T _ { i } = T _ { t o t }$ has been imposed in the energy efficiency controller, the required resultant torque increments in are set as zero. In this paper, Eq. (30) is transformed as a quadratic objective cost for optimization:

$$
\begin{array}{r l} J _ {\text {virtual}} & = (\mathrm{K} \Delta \varpi - \upsilon) ^ {T} \Xi (\mathrm{K} \Delta \varpi - \upsilon) \\ & = \Delta \varpi^ {T} \mathrm{K} ^ {T} \Xi \mathrm{K} \Delta \varpi - 2 \upsilon^ {T} \Xi \mathrm{K} \Delta \varpi + \upsilon^ {T} \Xi \upsilon \end{array}\tag{31}
$$

where $\Xi$ is a two-dimensional penalty weight matrix devoting to make $K \Delta \varpi - \upsilon = 0$ . From Eq. (31), the item $\boldsymbol { v } ^ { T } \boldsymbol { \Xi } \boldsymbol { \nu }$ is constant and independent of the optimized vector $\Delta \varpi$ , which can be removed without affecting optimization. Hence, Eq. (31) can be rewritten as

$$
J _ {\text {virtual}} = \Delta \varpi^ {T} \mathrm{K} ^ {T} \Xi \mathrm{K} \Delta \varpi - 2 \upsilon^ {T} \Xi \mathrm{K} \Delta \varpi\tag{32}
$$

2) Stability: Except the virtual controls regarding vehicle motion, the tire workload usage is also considered in this paper to improve the vehicle stability. It is a widely used index derived from the tire adhesion circle, by minimizing which the tire grip margin can be improved to handle suddenly adverse drive conditions [34]. The quadratic index of tire workload usage is:

$$
J _ {\text {stability}} = \varpi^ {* T} \Omega \varpi^ {*}\tag{33}
$$

where is a weight matrix equal to $\mathrm{diag}\left\{\frac{1}{\left(r_{w}\mu F_{zfl}\right)^{2}},\frac{1}{\left(r_{w}\mu F_{zfr}\right)^{2}},\frac{1}{\left(r_{w}\mu F_{zrl}\right)^{2}},\frac{1}{\left(r_{w}\mu F_{zrr}\right)^{2}}\right\}$ (29), Eq. (33) can be sorted as, $\begin{aligned}J_{s t a b i l i t y} = & \left( \boldsymbol{\varpi} + \Delta \boldsymbol{\varpi} \right)^T \Omega \left( \boldsymbol{\varpi} + \Delta \boldsymbol{\varpi} \right) \\= & \boldsymbol{\varpi}^T \Omega \boldsymbol{\varpi} + 2 \boldsymbol{\varpi}^T \Omega \Delta \boldsymbol{\varpi} + \Delta \boldsymbol{\varpi}^T \Omega \Delta \boldsymbol{\varpi}\end{aligned}$ . Since $\varpi ^ { T } \Omega \varpi$ is

independent of the optimized vector , it will not influence the optimization and can be removed. Thus, we have

$$
J _ {\text {stability}} = 2 \varpi^ {T} \Omega \Delta \varpi + \Delta \varpi^ {T} \Omega \Delta \varpi\tag{34}
$$

3) Energy Efficiency: Although adopting torques from energy efficiency controller can achieve the optimal economy in longitudinal drive cases, it cannot compromise with the indexes regarding stability, virtual controls, and series of constraints. To guarantee the energy efficiency of vehicle and minimize adjustments as possible, the energy efficiency index is set as

$$
J _ {\text {energy}} = \Delta \varpi^ {T} \Delta \varpi\tag{35}
$$

It is noteworthy that only summing up the above three objective costs for optimization cannot achieve the coordinated allocation of torque increments because the issue of addressed targets is a statically determinate problem; that $\dot { \mathbf { 1 } } \mathbf { S } _ { z }$ there are four costs (i.e., two of virtual controls, one of stability, and one of energy efficiency) and four control degrees of freedom (i.e., four torque increments) here. Therefore, the weighted sum approach is adopted to dynamically coordinate each target by $\mathrm { V W F } \left( \; \rho \; \right)$ . To arrange the priority orders of targets, the virtual controls are the top one to be satisfied which directly affect the vehicle motion. As to coordinate the performance of energy efficiency and tire workload usage, the VWF by dynamic control supervisor is delegated to play a role of weight coefficient in trading off these two targets in real time. Finally, the optimization objective in coordination torque allocator can be defined as

$$
J _ {C A} = J _ {\text {virtual}} + \rho J _ {\text {stability}} + (1 - \rho) J _ {\text {energy}}\tag{36}
$$

By Eq. (36), the allocator can adaptively provide the desired torque increments for the three expected targets. When vehicle has the trend of missing stability, $\rho$ from the supervisor will increase and tend to 1, by which the allocator prefers to minimize the tire workload usage for better vehicle stability. Instead, the energy efficiency effects are preferable for the allocator if the vehicle is stable $( \mathrm { i . e . , ~ } \rho   \to   0   )$

Besides the optimization objective, two constraints, i.e., physical limits of motor and tire adhesion limits, should be set up in the torque allocation, which aims to satisfy the motor traction capacity and tire adhesion safety requirements, respectively. The physical limits of four IWMs can be expressed according to Eqs. (11) and (29), as

$$
\begin{array}{c} \underline {{T _ {m}}} (\omega_ {m}) \times 1 _ {4 \times 1} \leq \varpi^ {*} \leq \overline {{T _ {m}}} (\omega_ {m}) \times 1 _ {4 \times 1} \\ \Rightarrow \underline {{T _ {m}}} (\omega_ {m}) \times 1 _ {4 \times 1} - \varpi \leq \Delta \varpi \leq \overline {{T _ {m}}} (\omega_ {m}) \times 1 _ {4 \times 1} - \varpi \end{array}\tag{37}
$$

where $1 _ { * _ { \times ^ { * } } }$ represents the $^ * \times ^ { * }$ matrix with all elements equal to one.

The tire adhesion limits are derived from tire adhesion circle theory for vehicle stability. By assuming $F _ { x i } \approx T _ { i } ^ { * } / r _ { w }$ the optimized torque increments should satisfy the following expression:

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \left(T _ {i} ^ {*} / r _ {w}\right) ^ {2} & \leq \mu^ {2} F _ {z i} ^ {2} - F _ {y i} ^ {2} \\ & \Rightarrow - \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z i} ^ {2} - F _ {y i} ^ {2}} \leq T _ {i} ^ {*} / r _ {w} \leq \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z i} ^ {2} - F _ {y i} ^ {2}} \end{array}\tag{38}
$$

By Eqs. (29) and (38), the constraint with respect to the torque increments for the four IWMs can be yielded as,

$$
\left| - \left[ \begin{array}{l} \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 1} {} ^ {2} - F _ {y 1} {} ^ {2}} \\ \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 2} {} ^ {2} - F _ {y 2} {} ^ {2}} \\ \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 3} {} ^ {2} - F _ {y 3} {} ^ {2}} \\ \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 4} {} ^ {2} - F _ {y 4} {} ^ {2}} \end{array} \right] \leq \frac {1}{r _ {w}} \varpi^ {*} \leq \left[ \begin{array}{l} \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 1} {} ^ {2} - F _ {y 1} {} ^ {2}} \\ \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 2} {} ^ {2} - F _ {y 2} {} ^ {2}} \\ \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 3} {} ^ {2} - F _ {y 3} {} ^ {2}} \\ \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 4} {} ^ {2} - F _ {y 4} {} ^ {2}} \end{array} \right] \right|\tag{39}
$$

$$
\Rightarrow - r _ {w} \left[ \begin{array}{l} \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 1} {} ^ {2} - F _ {y 1} {} ^ {2}} \\ \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 2} {} ^ {2} - F _ {y 2} {} ^ {2}} \\ \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 3} {} ^ {2} - F _ {y 3} {} ^ {2}} \\ \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 4} {} ^ {2} - F _ {y 4} {} ^ {2}} \end{array} \right] - \varpi \leq \Delta \varpi \leq r _ {w} \left[ \begin{array}{l} \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 1} {} ^ {2} - F _ {y 1} {} ^ {2}} \\ \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 2} {} ^ {2} - F _ {y 2} {} ^ {2}} \\ \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 3} {} ^ {2} - F _ {y 3} {} ^ {2}} \\ \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 4} {} ^ {2} - F _ {y 4} {} ^ {2}} \end{array} \right] - \varpi
$$

For optimization simplification, the above two constraints, i.e., Eqs. (37) and (39), can be merged:

$$
\max \left(\underline {{T _ {m}}} \left(\omega_ {m}\right) \times 1 _ {4 \times 1}, - r _ {w} \left[ \begin{array}{l} \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 1} ^ {2} - F _ {y 1} ^ {2}} \\ \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 2} ^ {2} - F _ {y 2} ^ {2}} \\ \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 3} ^ {2} - F _ {y 3} ^ {2}} \\ \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 4} ^ {2} - F _ {y 4} ^ {2}} \end{array} \right]\right) - \varpi \leq \Delta \varpi\tag{40}
$$

$$
\leq \min \left(\overline {{T _ {m}}} \left(\omega_ {m}\right) \times 1 _ {4 \times 1}, r _ {w} \left[ \begin{array}{l} \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 1} {} ^ {2} - F _ {y 1} {} ^ {2}} \\ \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 2} {} ^ {2} - F _ {y 2} {} ^ {2}} \\ \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 3} {} ^ {2} - F _ {y 3} {} ^ {2}} \\ \sqrt {\mu^ {2} F _ {z 4} {} ^ {2} - F _ {y 4} {} ^ {2}} \end{array} \right]\right) - \varpi
$$

Now, by Eqs. (32), Eqs. (34) to (36), and Eq. (40), the optimization problem in the coordinated torque allocator can be summarized and expressed in the form of convexquadratic programming:

$$
\begin{array}{r l} J _ {C A} & = J _ {\text {virtual}} + \rho J _ {\text {stability}} + (1 - \rho) J _ {\text {energy}} \\ & = \Delta \varpi^ {T} \left(\mathrm{K} ^ {T} \Xi \mathrm{K} + \rho \Omega + (1 - \rho) \times I _ {4 \times 4}\right) \Delta \varpi + \left(2 \rho \varpi^ {T} \Omega - 2 v ^ {T} \Xi \mathrm{K}\right) \Delta \varpi \\ & = \Delta \varpi^ {T} H \Delta \varpi + f \Delta \varpi \end{array}\tag{41}
$$

subject to Eq. (40), and $\left\{ \begin{aligned} H & = \mathbf{K}^{T} \Xi \mathbf{K} + \rho \Omega + (1 - \rho) \times I_{4 \times 4} \\ f & = 2 \rho \varpi^{T} \Omega - 2 \upsilon^{T} \Xi \mathbf{K} \end{aligned} \right.$

where $I _ { * _ { \times ^ { * } } }$ denotes an identity matrix with dimensions of $^ { * } \times ^ { * }$ . H and $f$ are the quadratic and first-order matrices, respectively. The optimization objective (41) is convexquadratic, and the constraints (40) are merged into one. Therefore, for faster optimization efficiency, a KKT optimal conditions-based method is adopted in this paper, which has been verified to yield excellent solving optimality and computational efficiency [44]. However, considering the limited space and study emphasis in this paper, the optimization steps are omitted in this paper. The interested readers can find more details in our previous contributions [2, 38].

After acquiring the optimal torque increments, the final torque commands of IWMs are calculated by Eq. (29) and input into DDEV (see Fig. 2).

**Remark 4**: In Eq. (40), $F _ { z i }$ can be calculated by vehicle load transfers functions [45], and then $F _ { y i }$ can be determined by the Magic Formula (4) and feedback vehicle information. The interested readers can find more details about accurate tire forces estimation in [46].

**Remark 5**: By (38), the tire forces can be bounded within tire adhesion circle, so that slipping can be avoided. More directly, one can impose the tire slip rate constraints to stabilize longitudinal motions, which can be expressed as $s_{\min} \leq s_{i}(0) + \dot{s}_{i} \Delta t \leq s_{\max} \cdot s_{i}(0)$ means the feedback tire slip rate of one tire, and denotes the sample step of the controller. $s _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ and $s _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ are the tire slip rate limits for drive safety. $\dot { S } _ { i }$ is the slip rate variant, which is determined by the IWM’s torque by the tire slip rate update function [2].

**Remark 6**: The VWF $\rho$ in Eq. (15) plays a key role to govern each target in handling-stability control (i.e., Eq. (18)) and torque allocator (i.e., Eq. (36)) between IWMs, as introduced in Section 3.1. As shown in Fig. 6 (b), when the unified index $I _ { u n i f i e d }$ is in the range of 0 to 0.7 which means that the vehicle state is within the stable region defined in the phase plane analysis, $\rho$ is zero and adopted in the following to increase the weight of targets like drive handling and energy efficiency. If $I _ { _ { u n i f i e d } }   >   1$ , from Eq. (18) and Fig. 6 (a), the vehicle is considered to lose stability, thereby $\rho ^ { - 1 }$ is set and applied in the handling-stability controller and torque allocator for vehicle stabilization. Considering the smoothness of coordination control, a transition stage of 0.3 is arranged in VWF to avoid control command chattering for expected drive comfort.

**Remark 7**: Actually, as shown in Fig. 6 (b), the gap of transition stage in Eq. (15) is adjustable and only required to be between 0 and 1, whose value is set as 0.3 since it is a relatively reasonable one to illustrate our strategy with ease in this paper. From Eqs. (13) to (15) and Fig. 6, one can find that wider transition stage means VWF will increase from zero with smaller $I _ { u n i f i e d }$ . Moreover, greater VWF denotes that the strategy is inclined to ensure vehicle stability rather than handling (see Section 3), and meanwhile more interferences will be paid by the strategy and deteriorate handling to some extent. Therefore, for novice drivers, the gap should be set greater to increase VWF for vehicle stability as early as possible, and instead it should be smaller to avoid needless interferences for experienced drivers. Additionally, with the development of V2X techniques, this gap value can be adjusted according to collected driver data by cloud communications with ease, thereby providing wider application potentials for the proposed strategy.

## 4.1. Control Performance

## 4.1.1. Longitudinal Drive Cases

In this subsection, four standard drive cycles are adopted for validating the energy efficiency effects, namely Urban Dynamometer Driving Schedule (UDDS), Highway Fuel Economy Test Cycle (HWFET), New European Driving Cycle (NEDC), and Worldwide Harmonized Light Vehicle Test Procedure Cycle (WLTC). The initial SOC is set to 0.9, the tire-friction factor is 1, and an even torque distribution strategy is employed for comparison.

Fig. 8 shows the inter-axle allocation results under WLTC cycle. From the middle subfigure, as discussed, the inter-axle allocation ratio fluctuates in the range 0.5 to 1. Front-wheeldrive appears to be more favourable for optimal energy efficiency during the last two highway drive sections. This can be explained as when speed is higher and smoother, the acceleration is small, so that the total traction torque is only in the range of 100 to 500 Nm, which cannot reach the switching ratio zones from 1 to 0.5 according to the optimal inter-axle allocation ratio map shown in Fig. 7. From the bottom subfigure of Fig. $^ { 8 , }$ the proposed method can effectively achieve energy consumption reduction, making up to 4945 W at 1571 s.

The energy efficiency comparisons between the proposed and even distribution methods are listed in Table III. Compared with even distribution method, the proposed one significantly improves the overall energy efficiency by 5.22% to 8.55 %. Notably, with the same initial SOC value of 0.9, the final SOCs increases by 0.55 % to 1.87 % through the proposed method. Moreover, compared with the even distribution method’s results, the energy-saving effects obtained through the proposed method are equivalent to reducing the vehicle mass by 91 kg to 173.5 kg, which is quite

difficult to be implemented during lightweight design.

## 4.1.2. Longitudinal and Turning Drive Cases

In this subsection, the double-lane-change (DLC) cycle is adopted to test the comprehensive performance of the proposed strategy, and two cases are studied: 1) Case 1: 100 km/h and tire-friction factor of 0.85; and 2) Case 2: 80 km/h and tire-friction factor of 0.4. Below the validations are divided into two parts to illustrate the superiorities of the proposed strategy, namely benefits in control reference and in DYC and torque allocation.

1) Control Reference: In this part, three control references, i.e., the proposed unified reference of Eq. (18), handling reference of Eq. (16), and stable reference of Eq. (17), are adopted in the proposed strategy to observe the coordination performance of handling and stability, while other settings are same.

Fig. 9 depicts the performance of three references under Case 1. From Fig. 9 (a), tracking three references can make vehicle stable because the lateral acceleration results are all within its adhesion limits, i.e., $\left| a _ { _ y } \right| \leq \mu g$ [34]. Given that the stable reference restricts the enlargement of sideslip angle for vehicle stability, its sideslip angle and lateral acceleration are lower than those of the other two references. However, this reference cannot contribute to enough handling effects for the driver. As shown in the bottom subfigure of Fig. 9 (b), the stable reference varies less than the other two for vehicle stability, but meanwhile entailing the understeer trend (see Fig. 9 (a)). To reduce the path tracking error, the driver attempts to sharply adjust the steering wheel, which leads to a worse handling experience. This can be seen in Fig. 9 (a) where the path tracking error is the greatest even if bigger amplitudes of steering angle have been imposed by the driver. From the top subfigure of Fig. 9 (b), by supervising vehicle motions (i.e., $\beta$ and $\gamma )$ , the VWF $( \rho )$ adaptively changes. At the first and third turn, the sideslip angles are greater, and the handling reference is closer to the yaw rate limit, thus the VWF increases to arrange the unified reference approaching stable reference for vehicle stability. Thanks to this, the smallest sideslip angle is achieved by the proposed unified reference, especially at around 2.5 s and 4.4 s, as shown in Fig. 9 (a), yielding the desirable vehicle stabilization. Meanwhile, compared with the handling reference, the vehicle handling is not weakened by the unified reference, which can be concluded via their similar path tracking and steering angle effects. Fig. 9 (c) shows the yaw rate tracking performance for the three references. With the considerations of tire nonlinearities in ITSM, the proposed strategy is able to effectively follow the target references.

Fig. 10 demonstrates the performance of the three references under Case 2. From Fig. 10 (a), the unified reference contributes to simultaneously achieve the smallest overshoots and steering angles in path tracking, which yields the best drive handling. For vehicle stability, the amplitudes of sideslip angle and lateral acceleration of the stable reference are smaller, but significantly greater steering angles and path tracking errors are caused, sacrificing the vehicle handling. Interestingly, one can find that the unified reference leads to smaller steering angle than handling references, which demonstrates the superior effects in drive handling. This can be explained as during turning, the handling reference cannot take the vehicle stability into account, thus entailing the extra steering burden for the driver to adjust vehicle motion. With the lower tire-road friction factor in Case 2, the unified reference is beneficial for a fine trade-off between handling and stability. As can be inferred from Fig. 10 (b), the developed supervisor effectively provides the appropriate VWF to switch between handling and stable references in time, so as to generate the unified reference to govern vehicle handling and stability in a synergistic manner. Moreover, owing to the smooth design of VWF in the transition stage (see Eq. (15)), no distinct vibrations occur with the unified reference, contributing to enhance the driving experience. Fig. 10 (c) shows the yaw rate tracking results under Case 2: the proposed ITSM controller can follow the references with smaller overshoots. At around 6.5 s, there are greater fluctuations when tracking the handling reference, because modelling errors are inevitable and increase in the tire nonlinear regions even if tire nonlinearities are considered in the ITSM controller.

2) DYC and Torque Allocation: To evaluate the effects of the proposed DYC and torque allocation, a classical LQR-based DYC with axle distribution (AD) of torques (named “LQR+AD” hereinafter) is implemented for comparison. For fairness, the proposed unified yaw rate reference is also adopted in the LQR controller, and the Bryson’s rules [47] are used for tuning the parameters. Since LQR is a linear control method, the linear tire model with same tire cornering stiffness of Eq. (16) is imposed. The AD torque allocation [25] is actually a rule-based method that distributes the IWMs’ torques according to the dynamic vertical forces of the tires, which can improve the tires’ grips and reduce the usage of motor power to some extent. This applied LQR+AD approach has been verified to be effective for energy saving and stability control in [25] and thus is helpful for the following discussions.

Fig. 11 illustrate the performance of the proposed and LQR+AD methods under Cases 1 and 2. From Fig. 11 (a) and (e), the proposed method yields superior effects in handling and stability, due to the smaller amplitudes in sideslip angle and steering angle, respectively. The vehicle stability of two methods can also be compared by the VWFs shown in Fig. 11 (b) and (f). With the same yaw rate reference settings, the VWFs in the LQR+AD method are greater than those obtained by proposed method. This implies greater risks of losing stability, also the unified reference tends to the stable reference for holding vehicle stability. The above advantages of the proposed method are attributed to its better yaw rate reference tracking capacity, shown in Fig. 11 (c) and (g). Compared with the linear control method (i.e., LQR), the proposed ITSM can take the tire nonlinearities into account and contributes to superior tracking performance. Fig. 11 (d) and (h) show the torque commands of IWMs and the tire workload usage. Compared with LQR+AD, the smaller tire workload usage is achieved by the proposed allocation, especially during the second and forth turns. To more intuitively assess the effects, Fig. 11 (i) illustrates the cumulative distribution function (CDF) results of tire workload usage for four IWMs. By using the proposed method, around 90 % of the time the overall tire workload usages are within 1.597 and 2.725, respectively for Case 1 and Case 2, that is significantly smaller than LQR+AD’s. This means that the proposed method has greater capacity to

To evaluate the energy efficiency effects, Fig. 12 illustrates the battery output power, power difference, and cumulative energy savings, by the proposed and LQR+AD methods. Under Case 1 and Case 2, the proposed strategy reduces the energy consumption by 0.001386 kWh and 0.0004283 kWh, respectively. From Fig. 12 (a), during turning, even if the virtual controls, tire workload usage, and energy efficiency, are all considered in the proposed strategy, it can still save 0.0009238 kWh. Under Case 2, with smaller tire-road friction compared with Case 1, a smaller feasible region is allowable in the torque increment optimization, which implies a smaller improvement in energy saving. Even so, the proposed method can also save 0.0002195 kWh during turning, as shown in Fig. 12 (b).

To further quantitatively evaluate the control effects, four performance indexes regarding handling, vehicle motion stability, energy consumption, and tire workload usage, are developed and introduced below:

1) Driver Workload (Handling): With the expected vehicle handling performance, less driver workload can achieve the desirable driving intention. Hence we adopt the driver workload index $E _ { h }$ calculated by integrating the magnitude of the steering angle to assess the vehicle handling [34]:

$$
E _ {h} = \int | \delta | d t\tag{42}
$$

2) Vehicle Motion Stability: The proposed vehicle stability evaluation index $I _ { u n i f i e d }$ in Eq. (15)can effectively reflect the vehicle stability status from Section 3.2. As to define the qualified effects through whole test cycles, $I _ { u n i f i e d }$ is integrated versus time to represent the stability performance. Thus the stability index $E _ { s }$ is expressed as

$$
E _ {s} = \int I _ {\text {unified}} d t\tag{43}
$$

3) Energy Consumption: The total energy depletion of battery (in kWh) is applied here as energy consumption index $E _ { e }$

$$
E _ {e} = \frac {\int P _ {b a t \_ {i} n} d t}{3 6 0 0 \times 1 0 0 0}\tag{44}
$$

4) Tire Workload Usage: As introduced in Section 3.5, the tire workload usage derived from the tire adhesion circle is expected to be minimized for countering the suddenly adverse drive conditions. Therefore, the overall tire workload usage integration versus time is arranged to verify stability in the torque allocation level:

$$
E _ {t} = \int (\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {4} \frac {F _ {x i} ^ {2} + F _ {y i} ^ {2}}{\mu^ {2} F _ {z i} ^ {2}}) d t\tag{45}
$$

where $F _ { x i }$ is the longitudinal force of the i-th wheel.

Fig. 13 depicts the performance comparison of above indexes by the proposed and LQR+AD methods. From Fig. 13 (a), the driver workloads by the proposed method are 4.98% and 4.21 % lower than those by LQR+AD method under Case 1 and 2, respectively, demonstrating the improved handling achieved by the developed strategy. From Fig. 13 (b), preferable effects of motion stability are yielded by proposed strategy, and one can find that its improvement under Case 2 is greater than that under Case 1, owing to the adaptive adjustments of VWF. In terms of energy efficiency, the proposed strategy completes two manoeuvres with lower electric energy consumption, making energy savings up to 4.64 % and 0.97 $\% ,$ respectively. The difference between savings under the two cases is attributed to the smaller feasible regions for managing vehicle motion and tire performance under lower tire-road friction road conditions. From Fig. 13 (d), the tire workload usage of the proposed method exhibits superior effects than LQR+AD’s, and the improvements are 9.87 % and 9.48 % under Cases 1 and 2, respectively. This means that a more moderate usage of tires is accomplished by the proposed method due to its appropriate coordination in multi-objectives torque allocation, which not only contributes to enhance vehicle stability, but also reduce tire wear hence slowing down tire aging.

## 4.2. Computational Time

The computational efficiency is a key factor for practical applications. Hence, we test the computational time of the proposed strategy under Case 1 and Case 2 here. All simulations are conducted through a desktop computer with 8 GB of RAM and a Core i5 processor of 2.90 GHz.

Fig. 14 demonstrates the results of computational time. Under the two cases, the computational time per sample is less than 0.00006 s and is greatly smaller than the sample time 0.01 s, yielding the real-time property of the proposed strategy. Given that the proposed strategy is conducted by interpolation of look-up tables and KKT-based optimization, the computational efficiency is significantly improved compared with the general methods (e.g. model predictive control, Newton algorithm-based torque allocation and so forth). Moreover, it is noteworthy that for torque control of

DDEVs in practice, the sample step is generally set as 0.05 s or more and is greater than that of 0.01 s in this paper. In other words, it can be deduced that the proposed strategy is realtime applicable in on-board computer for real-world vehicle experiments.

## V. CONCLUSIONS

In this paper, a supervisory control strategy of DDEVs is proposed to coordinate handling, lateral stability, and energy efficiency. It consists of a dynamic control supervisor, a handling-stability controller, an energy efficiency controller, and a coordinated torque allocator. The phase plane portrait analysis is conducted and delegated to determine accurate stability bounds that are stored as a look-up tables for online application. When driving, based on the current drive conditions and the vehicle states, a quantitative index of identified stable bounds is applied to generate the VWF for governing the supervisory strategy in real time. In the handling-stability controller, the VWF contributes to generate the unified yaw rate reference for trading off between handling and stability, and the nonlinear controller ITSM is employed for DYC to control the vehicle yaw motion. The energy efficiency controller determines the optimal inter-axle torques, and its effectiveness to find the globally optimal solution is strictly proved by PMP under the assumption of small battery power losses. The coordinated torque allocator is adopted to optimize the torque increments of each IWM with respect to the amounts provided by the energy efficiency controller, meanwhile minimizing the energy consumption and tire workload usage via VWF. Longitudinal and lateral drive manoeuvres are implemented to validate the control effects of the proposed strategy under CarSim-Simulink environment. Results verify the comprehensive improvements of control effects by the proposed strategy in handling, lateral stability, and energy efficiency, with respect to other methods. Moreover, the computational efficiency of the proposed method is tested, yielding the real-time potential for real-world vehicle experiments.

Under longitudinal drive cycles, i.e., UDDS, HWFET, NEDC, and WLTC, the proposed method yields improved energy efficiency by 5.22% to 8.55% compared with the even distribution method. The equivalent benefits of these energy savings are 91 kg to 173.5 kg reduction of vehicle mass, which is hard to be carried out in the structural design phase.

For longitudinal and turning test cases, the unified yaw rate reference can smoothly and timely switch between handling and steady-state objectives to effectively govern vehicle motion. By the proposed method, smaller yaw rate tracking errors and improved energy saving effects are achieved. For a quantitative evaluation of control effects, four performance indexes regarding handling, vehicle motion stability, energy consumption, and tire workload usage, are introduced. That allows to quantify the improvements of the proposed strategy in coordination of vehicle handling, stability, and energy efficiency, by comparing with LQR+AD method.

Future work will focus on the involvement of longitudinal stability control, real-world vehicle validations, and the robustness improvement of strategy against parameter uncertainties and external disturbances.

## APPENDIX A

Choosing the battery state of energy (SOE) as system state, the state update function is presented as

$$
S \dot {O} E = - P _ {b i} / E _ {b}\tag{46}
$$

where $E _ { b }$ is the maximum energy storage in the battery [48]. From Eq. (8), we have $P_{loss} = (P_{bi} / U_o)^2 R_o$ and

$$
P _ {b o} = P _ {b i} - P _ {l o s s} = P _ {b i} - (\frac {P _ {b i}}{U _ {o}}) ^ {2} R _ {o} \approx P _ {b i}
$$

Based on Eq. (47), the global optimization problem under a certain drive cycle can be defined as,

(47)

$$
\min \quad E _ {t o t} = \int P _ {b i} d t \approx \int P _ {b o} d t\tag{48}
$$

According to PMP [43] and Eqs. (46) to (48), the Hamilton function is expressed as,

$$
H = P _ {b i} - \lambda \frac {P _ {b i}}{E _ {b}} \approx P _ {b o} - \lambda \frac {P _ {b o}}{E _ {b}}\tag{49}
$$

where is the co-state variable, whose time derivation is $\lambda = - \frac{\partial H}{\partial S O E} = 0$ . The terminal condition of $\lambda$ is

$$
\lambda (t _ {e n d}) = \frac {\partial h}{\partial S O E} (t _ {e n d})\tag{50}
$$

where $h$ means the terminal cost in optimization problem, and $t _ { e n d }$ is the end moment of drive cycle. Since $h   =   0$ in problem (48), the expression $\lambda = 0$ is constantly hold. Thus, the Hamilton function can be rewritten as $H = P _ { b o }$ . From the optimality conditions in PMP [49], finding the globally optimal solution is equivalent to minimizing the Hamilton function at each discrete step. Therefore, the optimization of Eq. (48) is transformed to an instantaneous optimization of minimizing $H = P _ { b o }$ . In other words, $\int P_{bi}dt \Leftrightarrow \min P_{bo}$ is hold when $P _ { _ { l o s s } } \approx 0$
